title: Neighborhood-scale disparities in air exchange rates and inhaled pollution dose among school-aged children - Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology
description: Ambient air pollution and its infiltration into indoor environments can vary substantially within urban neighborhoods due to differences in traffic density, emission sources, and housing conditions; however, this variability is often not captured in exposure studies. This study estimates average daily inhaled dose of particulate matter (PM2.5) and ozone (O3) for school-aged children in Chelsea, MA, evaluating local differences in exposure. A hyperlocal network of 84 air quality monitors was combined with parcel-level housing data and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) infiltration model to estimate residential air exchange rates (AERs) and daily inhaled doses of PM2.5 and O3 across Chelsea. Across the city, average O3 daily doses ranged from 1.4 to 5.0 µg/kg, with ambient daily average concentrations varying by up to 39 µg/m3. For PM2.5, daily inhaled dose presented less variation, ranging from 0.52 to 1.4 µg/kg; however, observed spatial differences in median ambient PM2.5 concentrations of up to 4.4 µg/m3 were observed, which may still be sufficient to influence health outcomes. Residential air exchange rates (AERs) were higher in block groups with greater rent burden and larger Hispanic/Latino populations. The combination of parcel-level data and high-resolution monitoring revealed disparities in ambient concentrations, housing conditions, and inhaled dose that could meaningfully influence health outcomes in children.

outlet: U.S. Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
title: Whitehouse, McClellan Investigate EPA’s Decision to Exempt Data Center Power Plants from Acid Rain Protections
description:
EPA adopted new policy in response to lobbying from data center companies and in furtherance of Trump’s data center-over-people agenda 
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works (EPW), and Representative Jennifer McClellan (D-VA-04), last month launched a bicameral investigation into the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) guidance exempting data center power plants from the Acid Rain Program (ARP). 

By EPA’s own admission, the decision to issue new guidance came at the behest of data center companies.  And according to the EPA press release issuing the new guidance, the agency took this action to “further President Trump’s agenda promoting data centers.”

“EPA’s new ARP guidance is a handout to the richest and most powerful companies in the world.  And this handout comes at the expense of Americans’ health and the safety of our ecosystems and communities that were, prior to the inception of the ARP, regularly drenched in dangerous acidic rainfall,” the lawmakers wrote in their letter to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin.

The ARP regulates the emission of sulfur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) from power plants.  SO2 and NOx are both harmful to human health, damaging the respiratory system and worsening heart disease.  They are also linked to adverse pregnancy and birth outcomes, kidney damage, autoimmune disorders, and cancer.

The pollutants are also the primary causes of acid rain.  Prior to the ARP, acid rain poisoned rivers, lakes, and streams; damaged forests; killed and sickened aquatic animals; and corroded buildings, monuments, and statues.

“EPA explicitly bills its new guidance as a means to facilitate data center development.  In so doing, EPA misapprehends its own mission, which is to ‘protect human health and the environment,’ as stated in black and white on the agency’s own website,” continued the lawmakers.

“Bizarrely, under EPA’s new guidance, massive new gas-fired power plants large enough to power cities would be exempt from NOx and SO2 caps under the ARP only as long as they do not serve the public electricity grid and instead exclusively power a privately-owned data center.  This is a perverse outcome, and it is contrary to Congress’s design for the Clean Air Act, which creates specific and comprehensive regulatory requirements for significant pollution sources like these,” added the lawmakers.

The lawmakers, together with Senators Ed Markey (D-MA) and Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), requested answers from EPA by October 7th about the agency’s decision-making process while crafting this new guidance, as well as any information regarding the agency’s communications with data center companies.  Senators Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Cory Booker (D-NJ), and 24 Members of the House of Representatives also signed the letter.  EPA has not yet responded to the lawmakers’ letter.

Ranking Member Whitehouse also requested information and documents from the following companies by October 7th: Meta, Microsoft, Google, OpenAI, xAI, Amazon Web Services, Anthropic, Fermi America, and Joule. 

In March 2026, Ranking Member Whitehouse, Senator Van Hollen, and Senator Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, launched an investigation into eight technology and related companies, including Meta, xAI, and OpenAI, regarding twelve planned data center projects that would be powered by massive new gas plants.  The gas plants—many of which are ten or more times the size of the average gas plant currently powering the U.S. electric grid—would emit millions of tons of greenhouse gases and tens of thousands of tons of health-harming pollutants every year. 

The letter to EPA Administrator Zeldin is available here.

title: Lawsuit Challenges Trump EPA’s Failure to Cut Pesticide Pollution in Waterways, Drinking Water
description:
Conservation and public health groups filed a lawsuit today to force the Trump administration to develop required water quality standards for atrazine, a cancer-linked pesticide found at dangerous levels in thousands of U.S. waterways and in drinking-water supplies. 
Atrazine is the nation’s most widespread pesticide water pollutant. According to a new Center for Biological Diversity report, the pesticide contaminates 25% of all river miles in the continental United States at levels the Environmental Protection Agency recognizes as harmful to aquatic life. Atrazine pollution is caused by industrial agricultural operations using tens of millions of pounds of the pesticide each year.
Today’s lawsuit challenges the lack of water quality protections in American waterways as required under the Clean Water Act. The Act requires the EPA to develop water quality standards for pollutants like atrazine. The agency initiated but failed to complete that step in 1999.
